summary.text:
Wirral's annual report is the main report only — Appendices A to D are not held, so there is no CFR, no prudential indicator and no lender breakdown in what we have. The balance sheet identity cannot be closed from it and we assert nothing about it.

What can be checked, checks. Table 1 foots in every cell in both directions — eight independent sums, all exact — taking net debt from £512.78m at the half year to £591.37m at 31 March on £746.44m of borrowing added and £643.34m matured in six months. Loan debt is £472.11m, up £95m, with £65m of temporary local authority money (down from £84m) and £43.5m of LOBOs inside it.

Two things are distinctive. Their PWLB book is the only one we have priced that sits essentially at par: balance £314.2m against an indicative settlement of £315.0m, a net premium of £875,027, or 28 basis points. That is a consequence of shape — 30 of their 36 loans are EIP, the book is short and recently drawn at 4.4% to 5.4%, and there is almost nothing to reprice. Croydon's book carries £232.6m of discount and Bexley's £61.5m by comparison.

And paragraph 3.8 contains the only explicit statement we have read linking section 114 notices to inter-authority pricing — 'Tightening of the inter-authority lending market in the wake of increased issue of s114 notices also impacts loan market rates' — which is the mechanism behind the 4.0-4.5% normal against 5.0-7.0% year-end split their own 3.12 describes. The DSG deficit is named three times as a driver of the £95m increase in debt.

officer.body:
Hi [OFFICER NAME],

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on the annual report that went to Policy and Resources on 10 June. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

One caveat before anything else, so you know exactly what we did and did not see. We have the main report but not Appendices A to D, so we have no CFR, no prudential indicators and none of the debt detail in tables B1 and B2. That means we cannot close the balance sheet on your figures and we are not going to pretend otherwise, and it means the £472.11m cannot be decomposed from our side — £65m of it is temporary local authority money and £43.5m LOBOs, and the rest we can only see through our own PWLB file. Nothing below rests on a number we could not check.

What we could check, checks. Table 1 foots in every cell in both directions — four row sums and four column sums, eight in all, every one exact, carrying net debt from £512.78m at the half year to £591.37m at 31 March. That is worth saying because it is not the norm; summary tables of that shape usually have at least one rounding plug.

We wrote because of what your loan book looks like priced.

On the DMO's premature repayment curve this afternoon, your PWLB portfolio has a balance of £314.2m and an indicative settlement of £315.0m — a net premium of £875,027, or 28 basis points of principal. It is the only book we have priced that sits essentially at par. For context, on the same curve and the same afternoon, Croydon's carries about £232.6m of discount and Bexley's about £61.5m.

The reason is shape rather than luck. Thirty of your thirty-six PWLB loans are EIP rather than maturity, so 83% of the book by count is amortising rather than sitting whole until a bullet date; the weighted rate is 4.6792%; and the great majority of it was drawn recently, at 4.4% to 5.4%, against a repayment curve that today runs 4.0% to 4.6% across the tenors you hold. A book like that has very little in it to move away from par in either direction. Only two of your loans price below par at all.

We are not suggesting anything follows from that. We don't sell treasury products, we model no MRP or accounting treatment, and only the DMO can quote a real figure. It is worth a line because your own risk table makes the point correctly — "Higher interest rates can also improve debt rescheduling opportunities by increasing discounts/lowering premiums" — and in your case the rate rise has done neither, which is itself the answer to the question that sentence raises. Yours is priced daily at pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis.

The second thing is your paragraph 3.8, which contains a sentence we have not seen anywhere else: "Tightening of the inter-authority lending market in the wake of increased issue of s114 notices also impacts loan market rates."

That is the mechanism, stated plainly, behind what your own 3.12 then describes — local authority short-term borrowing at 4.0% to 4.5% for most of the year, rising to 5.0% to 7.0% towards the year end. We track that market across the sector because no council can see its shape from its own trades, and this year the range over the year end ran from 4.45% to 8.50%: Lancashire, Suffolk and West Northamptonshire lending at 4.45-4.50% in the same quarter that Cornwall paid 8.50% for four days and Harlow 7.75% for a month. Your £65m of temporary local authority borrowing, down from £84m, sits inside that distribution, and your report is one of the very few that explains why the distribution is as wide as it is. The month-by-month PWLB picture that sits alongside it — July was thin, £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02% — is at pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity.

Third, briefly. The DSG deficit is named three times as a driver: in the summary, at 3.6 as a reason net debt rose, and at 4.1 as the reason interest costs increased. Of the councils we have read this year, four others say the same thing in the same year — Wiltshire, Worcestershire, Herefordshire and Hertfordshire — and all of them are carrying it into a decision that does not sit with the treasury function. We mention it only because it is the one item in your report where the borrowing consequence and the service decision are furthest apart, and where a member reading the treasury report would not otherwise see the connection.

On training, four fit Wirral. PWLB repayment structures goes to the EIP weighting, and PWLB break costs — mechanics & live calculator to the par position above. Intra-LA borrowing & lending markets and LA Credit Analysis go to 3.8 and the £65m. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/

Russell
https://www.linkedin.com/in/russelltew

Source: Treasury Management Annual Report 2025-26, Policy and Resources Committee, 10 June 2026. Appendices A to D not held.
